titulo: Glasswing overwhelms maintainers with underwhelming findings (VulnCheck)
resumo: Patrick Garrity of VulnCheck has written a blog post that looks at vulnerabilities found by Anthropic's Project Glasswing since it launched on April 7, and finds it wanting: Of the 37,966 findings Anthropic reports, only 7,349 (19.4%) have been made public. Just 217 of those have been marked fixed. The more glaring number is that 4.4% (1,654) of the project's findings have already been marked as duplicates, 7.5x more duplicates than fixes. On top of that, 419 findings have been withdrawn. It seems odd that the ledger now claims a 94.2% true positive rate, up from 90.8% at launch, when more findings have been withdrawn or marked as duplicates than fixed, likely a feedback loop missing to the triage rates listed as "True Positives". [...] AI is a valuable tool for finding vulnerabilities, and I'm not discounting that. But seven months in, the evidence still doesn't match the launch narrative. The CVEs are a sliver of this year's total, almost none are being exploited, fixes have stalled while duplicates and withdrawals pile up, and the triage burden is shifting onto the open source maintainers Glasswing promised to help. The receipts keep coming in. They still don't reconcile.

titulo: [$] Additional hardening for the glibc dynamic linker
resumo: The Node.js project recently had a security vulnerability that affected its Brotli decoder. The bug was a buffer overflow , but the particular way that official Node.js binaries are built for Linux meant that one of the main protections against turning a buffer overflow into remote code execution, address space layout randomization (ASLR) could not be turned on. If ASLR had been enabled, the bug would still be exploitable in theory, but much more difficult to exploit in practice. In response, the GNU C Library (glibc) is considering a new set of tunable settings to allow administrators to forbid programs that do not support ASLR. The new settings, while a welcome hardening measure, may not address the root problem.

titulo: When Does It Actually Make Sense to Put AI Into Products?
resumo: Over the past few years, the tech industry has rushed to plug a new microchip into every device on the assumption that if you can add AI, you should. Smart-vision toothbrushes , mood-reading household robots , and a host of physical products are invading consumers’ daily lives, reliant on artificial intelligence to learn, predict, and adjust our behavior. But as anyone who’s struggled to update the firmware in their fridge knows, AI doesn’t improve every product. Some product designers are asking where the line is between genuine innovation and a solution looking for a problem. Savannah Kunovsky leads a team of industrial product designers at Ideo , a design consultancy based in San Francisco focused on helping clients unpack when AI becomes a barrier rather than a breakthrough. Kunovsky spoke with IEEE Spectrum about the pressure to integrate AI in everything, where that integration goes wrong, and what companies can do to determine when an AI integration is—and isn’t—a smart choice.
